pr_body:
This changes the HTTP/2's output processing to be use queues instead of locks (a channel to be precise). We're manually scheduling the Http2OutputProducer's intent to write instead of a write operation. This removes locks and allows the thread to do other useful work while processing in line for processing in a low allocation way.

Fixes #30235

~~Putting this up as a draft for now while I run performance tests and to get early feedback. ~~

issue_context.title: Improve HTTP/2 performance by using Channels
issue_context.body:
Today Kestrel locks and copies buffers into the connection pipe when multiplexing output from multiple streams. We could improve this by using a channel to queue writes to the pipe instead of locking (See https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/9a87636e7e5d767f2c1669b24f7fec86036442d3/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Http2/Http2FrameWriter.cs#L265 for an example).

This samples shows the difference between a `SemaphoreSlim` and a `Channel<byte[]>` and the performance difference is almost 3x with 0 allocations https://gist.github.com/davidfowl/8af7b6fa21df0fe1f150fb5cfeafa8f7.

There was still lock contention in Channels itself but it was pretty optimized.

We should prototype and measure this change.

cc @JamesNK @halter73 @Tratcher
comments:
Thanks for contacting us.
We're moving this issue to the `Next sprint planning` milestone for future evaluation / consideration. We will evaluate the request when we are planning the work for the next milestone. To learn more about what to expect next and how this issue will be handled you can read more about our triage process [here](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/docs/TriageProcess.md).

Note: The HTTP/2 FlowControl logic relies on being synchronized by the _writeLock.

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c925f99cddac0df90ed0bc4a07ecda6b054a0b02/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Http2/Http2FrameWriter.cs#L701-L715

We can instead move this logic into `WriterConsumer()` for synchronization, but that means TryUpdateStreamWindow will need to be an operation that can be written to the channel. That also means what looks like a single write to `WriteDataAsync()` could take several iterations of the `WriterConsumer()` loop to complete as the writes wait for flow control availability.

I don't think this causes a real problem for this approach. It's just a slight complication. I really like using Channels for this.

We've moved this issue to the Backlog milestone. This means that it is not going to be worked on for the coming release. We will reassess the backlog following the current release and consider this item at that time. To learn more about our issue management process and to have better expectation regarding different types of issues you can read our [Triage Process](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/docs/TriageProcess.md).

Evidence of this issue from gRPC benchmarks. They show:

* HTTP/3 is fast.
* H2C is slow.
* H2 (HTTP/2 + TLS) is even worse. I'm guessing it causes more time to be spent inside the lock and further increases thread contention. CPU usage on the server and client are both low.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/303201/130524768-c67b66cf-253f-4981-b443-0aaa5841bc95.png)

(h2 RPS is the yellow dot at the bottom)

review_comments: This is a small behavior change. Is the new behavior intentional?
Yes. There's no way to get a synchronous exception when writes are queued like this. I spoke to @Tratcher about it and he agreed this is fine.

We could preemptively check if any outgoing header values are longer than the current value of `Http2FrameWriter._maxFrameSize`. It makes this error a little clearer to the developer if it gets thrown directly to their app vs just showing up in the logs.

I don't think it's worth it though because we'd have to iterate over the response headers and additional time every request just for this validation.
This is the lock that was causing contention problems. Can it be removed?

Not fully. There will be less contention but window updates fire out of band from the normal processing so it's still required for that. Also writing 100 continue and probably some other obscure things (like ping frames)

Is this just for testing?

I don't think it needs to be fixed now, but I'd like to see this reworked to utilize `IHttp2StreamLifetimeHandler`. Tests should support customizing the handler so it can be used to raise this event. I did this in the HTTP/3 tests and it works well.

Can we avoid rescheduling if the reason for scheduling would be irrelevant before a connection window update? Like if we received a stream window update while waiting for a connection window update. Or if the app attempted to write more data or complete the response when the stream was already waiting for connection window availability.
I think `_isScheduled` is sufficient. I doubt the other case where we don't need to schedule because of lack of window are as common. If they are, we can optimize later.
Why the inconsistency between `CopyTo` in some places an foreaching over the data in others?

Change it to CopyTo everywhere. (I did this in my PR which was overwritten by this one 😢)

CopyTo has an optimized path for copying single-segment ROS.

I wonder if we would get any benefit from moving the operations above this line out of the `_writeLock` this is now never called by anything outside of `WriteToOutputPipe()`, right? It might be worth it in the trailers case where you already have the `_writeLock` from writing the previous frame, but it could be nice in the general case.
I believe that as long as only one HPACK header writer is operating at once (dynamic table is stateful) then it can happen outside of the write lock. Same scenario for writing headers and trailers.
Sure, this can be a follow up. My priority with this PR is to, avoid breaking anything and improve the performance.
Will file an issue for this.
Ok! I think leaving this as is right now is good. If profiling shows the lock no longer has much contention then it doesn't really matter.
